notes.detailedSummary: For r=|z|² in the chart z0=1, set ell=1-log r+log(1+r), a=alpha ell^(alpha-1), and b=alpha(1-alpha)ell^(alpha-2). The exact density is q_alpha=(1+a/r)^(k-1)(1-a+b/r). With p(r)=(r+a)/(1+r), its radial mass element is d(p(r)^k). The limits p(0)=0 and p(infinity)=1 prove total non-pluripolar mass 1. The asymptotic is r^(-k)(1-log r)^(-1-k(1-alpha)). notes.text:
This note proves B for every k>=2 and 0<alpha<1, using dd^c=i partial barpartial/(2pi), d^c=i(barpartial-partial)/(4pi), and kappa=dd^c log(1+|z|²) on z0=1. This normalization has integral kappa^k=1.

Write r=sum_{i=1}^k |z_i|², psi=log(r/(1+r)), ell=1-psi=1-log r+log(1+r), and chi(s)=1-(1-s)^alpha for s<=0. Set
 a=chi'(psi)=alpha ell^(alpha-1),
 b=chi''(psi)=alpha(1-alpha)ell^(alpha-2).
Both are positive, and a<=alpha<1. Off o,
 T:=kappa+dd^c u_alpha
   =(1-a)kappa+a dd^c log r+b dpsi wedge d^c psi.
Here dd^c log r is positive of rank k-1, and dpsi wedge d^c psi is positive. Thus T is strictly positive off o. The normalization used in the chain rule is dF wedge d^c F=(i/(2pi))partial F wedge barpartial F for real F.

The extension at o is genuine and canonical. A local potential for T is
 F(r)=log(1+r)+1-ell^alpha.
It tends to -infinity at r=0 and is locally integrable by radial integration. Its tangential and radial complex Hessian eigenvalues, after removing the common i/(2pi) factor, are
 F'(r)=(r+a)/(r(1+r)),
 F'(r)+rF''(r)=(1-a+b/r)/(1+r)^2.
They are positive. For each positive integer j, max(F,-j), extended as the constant -j sufficiently close to 0, is genuine psh on a coordinate ball. It is constant near 0 and a maximum of psh functions elsewhere. These functions decrease to F with value -infinity at 0. The psh mean inequalities pass to the decreasing limit, which is finite away from 0 and therefore not identically -infinity. Thus F is its canonical psh representative, and T is positive across 0. Subtracting log(1+r) gives the claimed genuine kappa-psh representative of u_alpha.

Globally psi<=0, with psi=0 on z0=0, so sup u_alpha=0. Its numerator vanishes exactly at o. Elsewhere psi is the logarithm of a smooth positive function, including along z0=0; composition with chi is smooth there. The sole pole is therefore o.

The Hessian eigenvalues of kappa are 1/(1+r) tangentially and 1/(1+r)^2 radially. Dividing gives the exact density
 q_alpha(r)=(1+a/r)^(k-1)(1-a+b/r).                 (1)
This is smooth and strictly positive away from o. The formula computes an intrinsic ratio of top-degree forms, so it defines the global density of T^k there.

The extended non-pluripolar measure agrees with this classical smooth product away from o and assigns no mass to {o}. Indeed on compact sets away from the pole the defining truncations eventually agree with the smooth potential. Non-pluripolar products and their smooth-background corrections discard the pole. It remains to check integrability and total mass.

Let p(r)=rF'(r)=(r+a)/(1+r). Differentiation gives
 p'(r)=(1-a+b/r)/(1+r)^2.
The normalized radial volume element of kappa^k is
 k r^(k-1)/(1+r)^(k+1) dr.
The complex radial Hessian determinant is (1+r)^(-k-1); Euclidean polar integration with the factor (i/(2pi))^k and the k! from the exterior power gives the displayed coefficient. Its integral is 1, also by differentiating (r/(1+r))^k. Substituting (1) shows that the radial mass element is
 q_alpha kappa^k = k p(r)^(k-1)p'(r) dr = d(p(r)^k). (2)
As r decreases to 0, a tends to 0 and p tends to 0. As r increases to infinity, ell tends to 1 and p tends to 1. Integration of (2) proves integrability and total extended mass exactly 1. The hyperplane at infinity has zero smooth volume, and the density extends smoothly across it, so integrating the affine chart loses no mass.

Put L=1-log r. Near 0, ell=L+log(1+r) is comparable to L, while a/r and b/r tend to infinity. Formula (1) therefore gives
 q_alpha comparable to a^(k-1)b r^(-k)
   =alpha^k(1-alpha) r^(-k)ell^(-1-k(1-alpha))
   comparable to r^(-k)L^(-1-k(1-alpha)).
The radial volume is comparable to r^(k-1)dr. The L1 integrand is comparable to r^(-1)L^(-1-k(1-alpha))dr, which is integrable. For every p>1 the Lp integrand is comparable to
 r^(k-1-kp)L^(-p(1+k(1-alpha)))dr,
which diverges since k-1-kp<-1. This proves the stated integrability assertions.

The same asymptotic shows uniform divergence q_alpha->infinity near o. Giving the density value infinity at o makes min(q_alpha,t) identically t in a neighborhood of o for every t>0. It is strictly positive and continuous globally. This density convention does not alter the potential, its canonical representative, or its pole.

For any compact Hermitian factor, the pulled-back radial solution satisfies the exact finite-mass equation with b_H(Rq_alpha)=binomial(m+k,m) integral h0^m. notes.detailedSummary: Lifting bounded factor potentials proves v_-(H)=0 when v_-(h0)=0. Closedness of h0 would contradict the bounded-product Stokes mass identity, so H is nonclosed. Smooth projective positive data have a smooth equation by the granted Tosatti-Weinkove corollary, with scalar fixed by Stokes. Lifting and smoothly sandwiching continuous data gives c_H(Rg)=D/integral g kappa^k, D=binomial(m+k,m)V0. Bounds r_-<=R<=r_+ squeeze the exact truncation scalars between D/integral min(q,j/r_-) and D/integral min(q,j/r_+). A direct computation off the inherited pole, followed by the defining absence of mass there, proves the actual unbounded product. No capacity convergence is inferred.
notes.text:
Let X0 be connected compact Hermitian of dimension m, h0 its metric, V0=integral h0^m>0, Y=P^k with k>=2, N=m+k, C=binomial(N,m), D=C V0, and H=h0+kappa on X0 x Y. Pullbacks are implicit. Let mu=(h0^m/V0) wedge kappa^k. For arbitrary smooth positive probability dV, R=mu/dV is smooth and positive, with 0<r_-<=R<=r_+<infinity.

A. Suppose v_-(h0)=0. Choose bounded genuine h0-psh v_j with masses tending to zero. Their pullbacks are bounded genuine H-psh. All differentials of v_j lie in the X0 directions. Multilinearity and degree counting give
 (H+dd^c v_j)^N=C (h0+dd^c v_j)^m wedge kappa^k.    (3)
For nonsmooth bounded potentials, add a smooth strictly psh quadratic dominating h0 on an X0 chart and convolve the corrected psh potential with radial kernels. Classical bounded local product convergence gives (3) after passage to the limit. The identity holds for the smooth approximants by the binomial expansion: terms with too many X0 or Y directions vanish. Integrating proves v_-(H)=0.

If h0 were closed, every bounded genuine h0-psh v would have total mass V0. In the bounded local product sense, (dd^c v)^j is closed and dd^c-exact, with primitive v(dd^c v)^(j-1). Distributional Stokes against the smooth closed h0^(m-j) annihilates every j>=1 term of the expansion of (h0+dd^c v)^m. Only integral h0^m remains. This contradicts v_-(h0)=0. Therefore h0 is nonclosed, and dH=pr0^*(dh0) is nonzero by restriction to an X0 slice. In dimension 1 the factor hypothesis is impossible by this same Stokes argument.

C. First suppose g is smooth and strictly positive on Y. Tosatti-Weinkove's permitted smooth theorem supplies a sup-normalized smooth v with kappa+dd^c v>0 and
 (kappa+dd^c v)^k=s g kappa^k.
The exact source is Corollary 1, printed page 1, https://arxiv.org/pdf/0910.1390v2; its closed-background normalization is printed page 2. The source operator is i partial barpartial, so its potential is multiplied by 2pi here. Its hypotheses hold: Y is connected compact, k>=2, and the background and data are smooth positive. Closedness and Stokes fix s=1/G, where G=integral_Y g kappa^k. Lifting v gives
 (H+dd^c v)^N=(D/G) Rg dV.
Uniqueness of the granted bounded normalization scalar gives
 c_H(Rg)=D/G.                                      (4)

For continuous strictly positive g, choose smooth positive g_l^-<=g<=g_l^+ converging uniformly to g. A finite chart cover, convolution and partition of unity provide smooth uniform approximants; adding or subtracting their approximation error enforces the inequalities and retains positivity. For bounded data, the granted maximal-subsolution characterization equals c, since sufficiently high truncations are unchanged. Consequently c decreases when the data increase. Applying this monotonicity to (4) for the smooth approximants proves (4) for every continuous strictly positive g. No additional nonsmooth projective existence theorem is needed.

Now let u be the canonical pullback of u_alpha and q=q_alpha from n1. Its pole is S=X0 x {o}. It is genuine H-psh because h0+(kappa+dd^c u)>=0. For f=Rq,
 integral_X f dV=integral_X q mu=1.
Moreover f is in L1 and in no Lp for p>1, since
 integral_X f^p dV=integral_X R^(p-1)q^p mu,
R^(p-1) has positive finite upper and lower bounds, and the projective integral diverges by n1.

Retain the exact truncations f_j=min(Rq,j). They are strictly positive continuous: q diverges uniformly near o and R>=r_-, so each f_j is identically j in a neighborhood of S. The pointwise inequalities are
 R min(q,j/r_+) <= f_j <= R min(q,j/r_-).            (5)
Indeed f_j=R min(q,j/R). Scalar monotonicity and (4) give
 D/integral_Y min(q,j/r_-) kappa^k
   <= c_H(f_j)
   <= D/integral_Y min(q,j/r_+) kappa^k.            (6)
Both denominators tend to integral q kappa^k=1 by monotone convergence. The original definition with min(f,j), the original reference dV, therefore gives
 b_H(f)=D>0.                                       (7)
This is not a replacement of min(Rq,j) by min(q,j).

Independently of this scalar limit, compute the extended equation. On X\S the potential is smooth, and block degree counting gives
 MA_H^ext(u)=C h0^m wedge (kappa+dd^c u_alpha)^k
           =C h0^m wedge q kappa^k
           =D f dV.                               (8)
The extended product has no mass on S: its defining non-pluripolar products discard that inherited pluripolar pole, and smooth-background corrections preserve this absence of mass. The right side has no mass on S either because it has an L1 density against a smooth volume. Equality off S thus proves equality of the actual measures everywhere. Its mass is D, finite. No scalar-to-potential compactness implication or unbounded limit-continuity theorem is used.

All of C, including (4)-(8), holds for every compact Hermitian factor; v_-(h0)=0 is used only in A. Thus C alone does not certify the named factor's collapse.

notes.detailedSummary: Take beta=(1+alpha)/2. Finite constants M_t=sup_{ell>=1}(1-t-ell^beta+t ell^alpha) and K_delta=sup_{ell>=1}(delta-1-delta ell^beta+ell^alpha) give a_t=u_beta-M_t and w_delta=delta u_beta-K_delta. notes.text:
Let h0 be any compact Hermitian factor, H=h0+kappa on X0 x P^k, and u_alpha the canonical pullback from n1. No factor-collapse assumption is needed for this note.

Fix alpha<beta<1, for example beta=(1+alpha)/2. By n1, u_beta is a genuine kappa-psh potential with the same sole pole and sup 0; its pullback is H-psh. Write ell=1-psi>=1, so off the pole u_alpha=1-ell^alpha and u_beta=1-ell^beta.

For every real t>=1 define
 M_t=max_{ell>=1}(1-t-ell^beta+t ell^alpha).
The maximum is finite because beta>alpha, and is nonnegative because the expression is zero at ell=1. The actual genuine H-psh potential
 a_t=u_beta-M_t
satisfies a_t<=t u_alpha. Thus a_t/t<=u_alpha, with both sides genuinely -infinity at S=X0 x {o}. Also u_alpha<=0, hence u_alpha preceq 0. These are precisely the supplied stretching requirements for E_env(X,H,0), with phi=0.

Explicitly, M_t=0 if t alpha<=beta. Otherwise differentiation locates the maximum at ell_t=(t alpha/beta)^(1/(beta-alpha)), giving
 M_t=1-t+t(1-alpha/beta)(t alpha/beta)^(alpha/(beta-alpha)).
This covers every t, not just a sequence.

For every 0<delta<1 define
 K_delta=max_{ell>=1}(delta-1-delta ell^beta+ell^alpha).
It is finite and nonnegative. The actual potential
 w_delta=delta u_beta-K_delta
satisfies w_delta<=u_alpha canonically, with value -infinity at S, and
 delta H+dd^c w_delta=delta(h0+kappa+dd^c u_beta)>=0.
It is the required genuine competitor. Explicitly K_delta=0 if delta beta>=alpha. Otherwise its maximum occurs at ell_delta=(alpha/(delta beta))^(1/(beta-alpha)), and
 K_delta=delta-1+(1-alpha/beta)(alpha/(delta beta))^(alpha/(beta-alpha)).

Here is an independent envelope-stability proof for the nonclosed background. Put theta=delta H, and let F be the family of genuine theta-psh v<=u_alpha. It contains w_delta and is uniformly bounded above by 0.

Finite maxima preserve theta-psh. On a coordinate ball convolve two potentials with nonnegative radial kernels. Distributional positivity gives
 dd^c(v_i*kernel)>=-(theta*kernel),
whose right side converges uniformly to -theta. Apply a smooth convex approximation of max to the two smoothed functions. Such an approximation is obtained by convolving max in its two real variables with a nonnegative compactly supported kernel. Its first derivatives are nonnegative and sum to 1, its real Hessian is positive semidefinite, and it tends uniformly to max. The complex Hessian chain rule therefore preserves the lower bound -(theta*kernel). Local L1 convergence of the smoothed potentials and the Lipschitz property of max give local L1 convergence to max(v1,v2). The distributional inequality passes to the limit. A common local smooth quadratic rho with dd^c rho>=theta makes both v_i+rho psh and commutes with max, so the actual usc maximum is its canonical representative. This proves closure without a global regularization theorem.

Choose a countable basis of relatively compact coordinate balls B_l and put s_l=sup_{v in F}sup_{B_l}v. Each s_l is finite: the family is bounded above, while the competitor is finite somewhere in every open ball. For each l and positive integer j choose v_{l,j} in F with sup_{B_l}v_{l,j}>s_l-1/j. Enumerate these functions and let b_J be their first J finite maximum together with w_delta. Then b_J is genuine theta-psh, increases, and satisfies
 w_delta<=b_J<=u_alpha<=0.
Since w_delta is locally integrable, dominated convergence gives an L1 limit b. The inequalities theta+dd^c b_J>=0 pass to distributions.

Locally b_J+rho is an increasing family of psh functions bounded above. Its canonical psh limit is the usc regularization of the pointwise limit. This follows directly from the mean inequalities: the regularization is bounded above by the limits of small-ball averages, which recover the canonical distributional representative; conversely every b_J+rho lies below that representative, and taking J to infinity and regularizing gives the reverse inequality. Denote b's canonical representative by b*. It is genuine theta-psh.

The countable selection has the same supremum on every basis ball as the whole family: sup_{B_l}b=s_l. Taking shrinking neighborhoods therefore gives
 b*=(sup_{v in F}v)^*=P_theta(u_alpha).
Because u_alpha is usc and bounds every member above, it also bounds the regularized supremum above at every point. Hence the envelope has its actual value -infinity on S. Off S it lies between the finite w_delta and finite u_alpha, and is finite there. It is not identically -infinity. Thus P_(delta H)(u_alpha) is a genuine delta H-psh potential for every delta, proved through the actual competitor.

The local canonical-Hessian foundation checked is Demailly I.5.8-5.9, printed page 40, https://people.math.harvard.edu/~demarco/Math274/Demailly_ComplexAnalyticDiffGeom.pdf. The nonclosed maximum and envelope arguments above are reconstructed rather than imported.

notes.text:
This note proves the named quotient's geometry, metric and volume, and records a proved failure of one collapse approach. It does not prove E's mass-collapse clause.

Let z=(z1,z2), w=(w1,w2), Omega={ [z:w] in P3 : z!=0, w!=0 }, q=exp(2pi), and g[z:w]=[z:qw]. The holomorphic map pi([z:w])=([z],[w]) to P1 x P1 has fiber C*. On a base chart z_i!=0, w_j!=0, normalize z_i=1, use zeta for the other z coordinate, write w=s(1,eta) with w_j=s, and take s=w_j/z_i!=0. This is a holomorphic product chart C x C x C*. Switching coordinates changes s by the nonvanishing holomorphic multiplier (w_{j'}/w_j)/(z_{i'}/z_i). The deck action is s->qs.

The globally smooth t=log(||w||²/||z||²) satisfies t(gx)=t(x)+4pi. The action is free. It is properly discontinuous because compact sets have bounded t ranges, so only finitely many translates can meet another compact set. Small neighborhoods of t width less than 4pi provide local holomorphic quotient charts, giving a smooth Hausdorff threefold X0.

On each base trivialization the quotient is U x E, where E=C*/q^Z=C/(2pi Z+2pi i Z) under s=exp(x+iy). The transition multipliers give holomorphic translations of E. The strip 0<=t<=4pi is compact in P3 and contained in Omega: after normalizing ||z||²+||w||²=1, its ratio bounds keep both norms uniformly positive. Every orbit meets this strip, proving compactness. The base and fiber of Omega are connected, so Omega and its quotient are connected.

Let A=alpha0 and B=beta0 be the pulled-back area-one Fubini-Study forms. In the ratio chart,
 t=log|s|²+log(1+|eta|²)-log(1+|zeta|²),
so dd^c t=B-A=:S. The deck-invariant forms dt and d^c t descend. Put eta0=dt wedge d^c t=(i/(2pi))partial t wedge barpartial t, a positive rank-one form. Its vertical component is nonzero because partial t=ds/s vertically. Together A, B and eta0 have independent complex covectors. Thus omega=A+B+eta0 is descending and strictly positive.

Exterior differentiation gives d omega=-dt wedge S, which is nonzero: the horizontal A and B directions and the vertical dt direction are independent. Hence omega is genuinely nonclosed.

Since A²=B²=eta0²=0,
 omega³=6 A wedge B wedge eta0.                    (9)
On each fiber, t=2x+constant, d^c t=dy/(2pi), and eta0=dx wedge dy/pi. Both x and y have period 2pi, giving integral_E eta0=4pi. Horizontal components disappear after wedging with A wedge B. Fiber integration in the explicit bundle charts gives
 integral_X0 omega³=6 (integral_P1xP1 A wedge B)4pi=24pi. (10)
All normalization factors are retained.

There is an exact smooth mass identity. Direct differentiation gives
 dd^c omega=-S²=2 A wedge B,
 d(omega²)=-2dt wedge (A+B) wedge (B-A)=0.
Thus dd^c(omega²)=0. For any smooth real u, Stokes gives
 integral (dd^c u)^3=0,
 integral omega² wedge dd^c u=0,
 integral omega wedge (dd^c u)^2
   =integral u dd^c u wedge dd^c omega
   =-integral du wedge d^c u wedge dd^c omega.
The final equality follows by integrating d(u d^c u wedge dd^c omega), since dd^c omega is closed. Expansion yields
 integral (omega+dd^c u)^3
   =24pi-6 integral du wedge d^c u wedge A wedge B. (11)
For strict positivity the mass is positive and the energy is less than 4pi. A smooth collapse sequence would require energies approaching 4pi. Identity (11) does not supply such a sequence.

Consider the restricted approach u=a(t), with a smooth of period T=4pi. Put p=a'; p is periodic with mean zero. Then
 omega+dd^c u=(1-p)A+(1+p)B+(1+p')eta0.
Strict positivity is equivalent to -1<p<1 and p'>-1. Fiber integration and periodic integration by parts give
 integral (omega+dd^c u)^3
   =6 integral_0^T(1-p²)(1+p')dt

For a positive closed current T of bidimension (p,p) on a complex manifold and c>0, {x:ν(T,x)≥c} is analytic of dimension at most p (Siu; Demailly III.8.5).

On a compact complex d-fold, a smooth real (1,1)-form θ, not necessarily closed, admits a real distribution v with θ+dd^c v≥0 if ∫θ∧Θ≥0 for every smooth strictly positive dd^c-closed (d−1,d−1)-form Θ (Lamari, Lemma 3.3).
On an open Ω⊂C^d, a real distribution with positive complex Hessian has a unique locally integrable genuine psh representative (Demailly I.5.8).
